passages.title: The fleeing prophet meets sailors who try to save him
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jonah to go and preach against the great city of Nineveh. Jonah boards a ship going the other way. The LORD sends a violent storm. The sailors pray to their gods and throw the cargo overboard. Jonah is asleep below. The lot points to him, and he tells them to throw him in. The men row hard for land and then do as he says. The sea grows calm, and a great fish swallows Jonah.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate the port and city named in the story. The sea journey is not reconstructed.

lds.text: The 2026 lesson reads the rescue as another opportunity for Jonah to respond. How do the sailors’ actions contrast with Jonah’s flight?

contextNote.title: The fleeing prophet meets sailors who try to save him
contextNote.text: The foreign sailors behave better than the prophet. They pray while he sleeps (verses 5–6). He tells them to throw him overboard. Verse 13 says they rowed hard for land instead. They risked themselves for the man who had endangered them. In verse 14 they ask not to be guilty of his blood. Verse 16 ends with the sailors worshiping the LORD.

passages.title: A rescued voice thanks the God it tried to flee
passages.summary: Jonah prays to the LORD from inside the fish. He says he called from the depths, and God heard him. The waters closed over him, and weeds wrapped his head. He sank to the roots of the mountains. God brought his life up from the pit. Jonah says idol worshipers give up their hope of mercy. He will offer thanks and pay his vows. The LORD speaks to the fish, and it puts Jonah on dry land.
passages.uncertainty: The fish’s location and the point of return to land are not given.

lds.text: The lesson invites readers to notice God’s mercy throughout Jonah’s experience. How does Jonah’s promise compare with the sailors’ earlier worship?

contextNote.title: A rescued voice thanks the God it tried to flee
contextNote.text: Jonah’s prayer is a psalm of thanks. He speaks it inside the fish, which he counts as his rescue. He says nothing about Nineveh or about running away. In verse 8 he looks down on those who worship idols. The sailors of chapter 1 have just worshiped more truly than he did. Verse 9 ends, “Salvation belongs to the LORD.” In chapter 4 he resents that truth when Nineveh receives it.

passages.title: A brief warning produces a citywide change
passages.summary: The LORD’s word comes to Jonah a second time, and he goes. He walks a day into the city. He says that in forty days Nineveh will be overthrown. The people believe God and put on sackcloth. The king leaves his throne and sits in ashes. He orders everyone to fast, pray, and turn from violence. He says God may yet relent. God sees that they have turned, and he does not destroy them.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate the port and city named in the story. The sea journey is not reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson connects Nineveh’s change with sharing the gospel despite uncertain expectations. Why does God’s response focus on changed conduct?

contextNote.title: A brief warning produces a citywide change
contextNote.text: Jonah’s message in verse 4 is one sentence with no offer of mercy. The whole city responds, from the king down. Verse 8 defines what turning means. Each person must leave his evil way and the violence in his hands. The king presumes nothing and says God may relent (verse 9). Verse 10 says God saw their works. Jeremiah 18:7–8 states the rule that a warned nation may be spared.

passages.title: Concern for a plant meets concern for a whole city
passages.summary: Jonah is very angry that Nineveh is spared. He says this is why he fled in the first place. He knew God is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger. He asks to die. He sits outside the city to see what will happen. God gives him a plant for shade and then sends a worm to kill it. Jonah is angry enough to die. God asks whether he should not care for a great city and its animals.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate the port and city named in the story. The sea journey is not reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson asks readers to consider mercy toward others when Jonah resents their rescue. Whose lives does God include in the final question?

contextNote.title: Concern for a plant meets concern for a whole city
contextNote.text: Verse 2 finally explains why Jonah ran. He knew God’s mercy and did not want Nineveh to receive it. He quotes Exodus 34:6 as a complaint. The plant shows what Jonah cares about. He pities a vine that gave him shade for a day. God’s question in verse 11 sets that beside a whole city. The book ends with the question, and Jonah gives no answer.
